comments.author: @TheApeMachine
comments.text: It's actually interesting. A different, but conceptually similar, thing I noticed with Claude 3.7 where, yes, it is definitely even better at writing code than it was before, however, it is also completely out of control in how it does the implementation. I've been writing my own agent framework, and before, Claude would use existing libraries always, because that just makes common sense. As soon as I started to use 3.7, it started to re-implement everything as raw HTTP calls to the OpenAI API, and also just vomiting so much code all over the place. Like an insane amount, just to do something that after I cleaned it all up, only 10% was actually needed. It's interesting, because we always talk about "scaling laws" as if it is just one line of effect going up, but the truth is, it's many lines of effect, which all have their side-effects, which all influence each other. So what if those become significantly misalinged? For instance, I once heard a story about this Russian woman who was able to remember every chess game, and every chess position she had ever been in, but lost the ability to recognize people's faces. You know what I mean? Maybe only some elements can scale up, maybe the architecture cannot support a certain level of scale, etc. This stuff is so much more complex than it seems, especially on the drunkeness of the hype after what has been a real significant moment of success, and a true breakthrough after a very long time. Or, maybe we'll have AGI soon, who knows. I'm just saying, it took evolution quite a while to make something robust enough that if you damage a large part of it, it still kind of works (the brain I mean). While if I put one LLM param like top_p or something 0.2 steps out of position I get a model that just spews random shit :p

comments.author: @shadfurman
comments.text:
Only about halfway through... 

There's a lot more that goes into the intelligence of a model than just the size of the model. The type of training and the training data also play a big part, but it's even more than that.

If the model is too large relative to the data, the model will overfit, basically just memorize large amounts of the data. This doesn't make it smarter. You WANT the model to be forced to compress the data into heuristics, that's what "understanding" is.

There's also the length of training. If you cut the model off when it reaches the peak of the first maxima output, the efficiency will be under utilized. This is largely because the first layers are still mostly random. The training hasn't "reached" that deep into the model yet.

A deep NN doesn't tend to get "stuck" like smaller models do, it has enough points of dimension to work around local minima in the layer to find a more efficient path. 

It can take 100s or 1000s of times longer, but the model will likely find a more efficient route to prediction as the first layers are adjusted minute amounts, but then, after insane amounts of training, magic (usually) happens, it starts getting better again and then this time it levels off.

The bigger the model, it takes exponentially longer to "learn", so to reach that point could take many years of training, even with more GPUs.

I expect they released 4.5 early, maybe not realizing how underperforming it still was, but still necessary to look like they're still making advancements. They'll also need 1000x the amount of data to reach an optimal saturation.

There really isn't a data shortage. They don't want incoherent data, but they don't need just text either. They can use many sources of coherent data, such as video, or even (I'm pretty sure) even executable files would work (they are coherent if they're not too buggy.)

If this numbering scheme is accurate, I expect 4.5 will continue getting better, and when the model reaches the grok point (that magic moment where it actually understands ie 4 - 4o) that will be a new release.

But then they also have to RL train it for reasoning. That is the end point of the model.

Alternatively, they could generate synthetic data, such as how xAI is doing, or just skip to a reasoning model and RL the shit outta it for years.
They might be planning to skip some steps they did before now that they know more, there might be a more effecient path to the end result. 

There are many options, but I don't think 4.5 is really intended to be a new model, it's just the interim of a bigger model that will become the new model.

I don't think they're so stupid to mistake 4.5 as the next big thing, yet. I don't think it's likely they just made a mistake.

Perhaps they need the feedback data to train it further before the next step, so they had to release it so people would interact with it.
(But if that's the case, I don't think they'd pay wall it. On the other hand, maybe the pay wall is temporary, or an intential bottle neck since they're limited on servers and the training is slower.)
